paper.title: Overcoming obstacles to innovation: Can an educated workforce help?
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement appears in the article. …

registers.years: 2006-2018 (2018 wave is the main source; earlier waves 2006-2015 used for the willingness-to-innovate screen)
registers.role: outcomes (innovation), obstacle variable (selection equation), some controls (R&D costs, external R&D, collaboration), sample frame

registers.name_in_paper: registry data (Statistics Denmark); 'registry data information on the firms' number of employees, export shares, age, market power, industry, geographic area, financial vulnerability, and workforce education'
registers.role: treatment (workforce education / skill intensity and educational diversity) and controls

linkages: survey data merged with registry data using firm and worker identifiers
workers linked to firms, so that education, age and tenure can be aggregated to firm-level shares and standard deviations

sample.universe: Danish manufacturing and service firms responding to the 2018 wave of the Community Innovation Survey, a mandatory survey sent each year by Statistics Denmark to a new group of firms selected as a representative sample of all Danish firms
selection_rules: Start from the CIS 2018 wave, which reports innovation and obstacles for the period 2016-2018

Exclude firms classified as not interested in innovation: no innovation activities or obstacles reported in 2016-2018 AND no innovation activities reported in 2006-2018; this excluded 12 % of the original sample and left 2604 firms
Exclude firms lacking educational information or other information used in the empirical analysis, leaving 2223 firms
sample.period: 2006-2018; innovation outcomes and obstacles for 2016-2018; firm and worker characteristics from 2015
sample.n_observations: 2223 firms (642 not facing obstacles, 1571 facing obstacles, per Table A1)

construction_notes: Skill intensity = the share of the firm's workers with at least 14 years of education, measured in 2015 (written skill_{it-3}).
Each obstacle question is answered on a four-point scale (1 great importance, 2 some importance, 3 little importance, 4 not relevant); a dichotomous variable takes the value 1 for answers 1 or 2.
Three obstacle-type dummies (money, knowledge, market) plus an overall indicator equal to 1 if the company reported at least one of the 9 obstacles.
Innovation: three type dummies (product, service, process), each 1 if at least one of the underlying CIS questions is answered yes, plus an overall innovation dummy.

In Tables 9, A12 and A13 the obstacle variable becomes an ordered variable: 0 = no obstacles, 1 = only the column's obstacle type, 2 = the column's obstacle type plus at least one other; firms that face only obstacles outside the column's type are dropped.

Educational diversity indices follow Eq. (5), Index_it = 1 - sum_s p_ist^2, computed over four educational-background categories (horizontal) and over unskilled, skilled, short (14 years), medium (15-17 years) and long (18 years or more) education (vertical).
Age diversity and tenure diversity are the standard deviations of worker age and tenure within the firm.

The Herfindahl-Hirschman index is the sum over industry of the square of a firm's Danish sales divided by total industry sales, with industry at the six-digit level; the Lerner index is 1 minus the industry mean of results divided by sales.
Industry is classified by DB07, the Danish version of NACE rev. 2, at the six-digit level, grouped into 22 industry dummies.
R&D cost is Ln(R&D and innovation costs in 2018 per employee), in DKK.
All regressions are unweighted; the stratification variables (size, industry, past R&D expenditure level and variance) are included as controls instead.

links.pointer_quote: Interestingly, we find that increasing skill intensity has no impact on the likelihood of innovation for firms that do not face obstacles.

claims.statement: Among firms not facing obstacles, skill intensity has no statistically detectable effect on innovation success (inno_it) (coefficient .13, not significant at the 10 % level).

definition.value: Share of the firm's workers with at least 14 years of education, measured in 2015 (denoted skill_{it-3}, lagged relative to the 2016-2018 innovation window), from Statistics Denmark register data merged to the survey by firm and worker identifiers.

timing.value: Measured in 2015, the year preceding the 2016-2018 window over which the innovation outcome and obstacles are reported, written skill_{it-3} in Eqs. (1)-(3).

definition.value: Dichotomous variable equal to 1 if firm i at time t had product, service and/or process innovation in 2016-2018, 0 otherwise. Built from nine CIS survey questions: three dummies (product, service, process) each equal to 1 if at least one question within that innovation type is answered yes, plus an overall dummy equal to 1 if at least one question across the innovation types is answered yes.

timing.value: Reported in the 2018 wave of the Community Innovation Survey for the period 2016-2018.

units.value: change in the probability of innovation per one-unit increase in skill intensity, i.e. moving the share of workers with at least 14 years of education from 0 to 1

estimand.target_population: Danish manufacturing and service firms in the CIS 2018 estimation sample, restricted to firms that do not face obstacles to innovation (the obstacles = 0 regime, Eq. (2)), on the full estimation sample of 2223 firms.
estimand.time_horizon: Innovation outcomes over 2016-2018, with skill intensity and the other firm characteristics measured in 2015 (one to three years earlier).
estimand.formal_query: E[Innovation success (inno_it) | do(Skill intensity = s+1), firms that do not face obstacles to innovation (the obstacles = 0 regime, Eq. (2))] − E[Innovation success (inno_it) | do(Skill intensity = s), firms that do not face obstacles to innovation (the obstacles = 0 regime, Eq. (2))]

population.description: Danish manufacturing and service firms in the 2018 wave of the Community Innovation Survey merged with Statistics Denmark register data, excluding firms with no declared intention to innovate and firms lacking educational or other information used in the analysis; here firms that do not face obstacles to innovation (the obstacles = 0 regime, Eq. (2)), on the full estimation sample of 2223 firms.
population.period: Innovation outcomes and obstacles 2016-2018; firm and worker characteristics 2015; earlier CIS waves 2006-2015 used for the willingness-to-innovate screen.
subgroups_defined: firms facing obstacles vs firms not facing obstacles
population.selection: Statistics Denmark draws the CIS sample as a representative, stratified sample of all Danish firms (stratified by firm size, industry and past R&D expenditure, level and variance). Firms with no declared intention to innovate (12 % of the original sample) and firms lacking educational or other information were then dropped, leaving 2223 firms; this column conditions further on firms that do not face obstacles to innovation (the obstacles = 0 regime, Eq. (2)).

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between firms in the share of their 2015 workforce with tertiary education, within 22 industries and conditional on firm characteristics. There is no reform, lottery or discontinuity; the endogenous switching regression (Lokshin & Sajaia, 2004) corrects only for the non-random selection of firms into the regime of facing obstacles, via a probit selection equation and an inverse Mills ratio.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the included firm characteristics, the 22 industry dummies and (in the innovation equations) the inverse Mills ratio, lagged skill intensity is independent of the unobserved determinants of innovation success (inno_it).
key_assumptions.supported_by: No direct test. The paper argues that lagging the explanatory variables to 2015 reduces simultaneity bias and that controlling for industry already accounts for unobserved industry-specific differences related to both skill intensity and innovation.

rhs: unobserved determinants of Innovation success (inno_it)

key_assumptions.assumption: Facing obstacles is endogenous, so each regime's estimation sample is selected; the innovation-equation errors are allowed to covary with the obstacle-equation error and the selection is corrected by the inverse Mills ratio from the probit Eq. (3).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eq. (4) sets Cov(e1it,uit) = sigma_1u != 0 and Cov(e0it,uit) = sigma_0u != 0; Table 6 reports sigma_1u = -0.22 and sigma_0u = -0.38, which the paper reads as demonstrating the need to correct for selection bias.

implies_edges.to: estimation sample conditioned on the obstacle regime

formal.as_written: Cov(ε1it, uit) = σ1u ≠ 0 and Cov(ε0it, uit) = σ0u ≠ 0

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction for the selection correction: ln(sales), import share, collaboration with universities and with consultants, and the nine Lerner-index dummies determine the probability of facing obstacles but do not enter the innovation equations directly.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 4 argues that the HHI affects innovation but not whether a firm faces obstacles, while a high Lerner index (low profit margin) affects whether firms face obstacles; no formal test of the exclusion is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The explanatory variables are predetermined: skill intensity and the other firm characteristics are measured in 2015, before the 2016-2018 innovation window, so innovation outcomes do not cause the measured skill intensity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the reason for using lagged explanatory variables; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on firms having a declared intention to innovate; firms with no innovation activities or obstacles in 2016-2018 and no innovation activities in 2006-2018 are dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A7 column 1 re-estimates the model without deleting firms that are not willing to innovate and reports the same findings.

implies_edges.to: estimation sample conditioned on willingness to innovate

key_assumptions.assumption: Distributional and functional assumptions of the endogenous switching model: a linear index in each equation and joint normality of the error terms, as required by the probit selection equation and the inverse-Mills-ratio correction.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the two-step consistent estimator of Heckman (1979) is used and that the findings are the same under full maximum likelihood; the distributional assumption itself is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is a stratified draw: Statistics Denmark selects CIS firms by size, industry and past R&D expenditure, and the regressions are run unweighted with the stratification variables included as controls.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 1 and footnote 7; footnote 7 reports that weighted versions of Tables 6 to 8 give similar results.

threats_discussed: non-random selection into facing obstacles (sample selection bias in which firms face obstacles)
simultaneity bias: a firm's innovation performance can affect which workers it hires
selection bias from asking firms that were not willing to innovate about their obstacles to innovation
using innovation activities rather than innovation outcomes as the dependent variable, since some firms do not report their innovation activities
robustness_checks: Table 7: re-estimation on manufacturing, service, low-tech, publishing and medium-/high-tech sub-samples
Table 8: re-estimation on sub-samples split at 45 million DKK of sales and at 30 employees
Table A7 column 1: firms that are not willing to innovate are kept in the sample
Table A7 column 2: firms that did not report innovations in 2008-2018 are deleted instead
Table A7 columns 3 and 4: alternative constructions of the dichotomous obstacle variable (great importance only; great, some or low importance)
Table A6: skill intensity entered as four dummies with firms with no educated workers as the base
Footnote 7: the regressions in Tables 6 to 8 re-run on a weighted sample with similar results (not reported)
Table 6 note: the findings are the same if using the full maximum likelihood estimator instead of the two-step consistent estimator
unresolved_confounders: the authors state that more definitive causal inference could possibly be obtained by using a suitable natural experiment, field experiments or larger panel datasets
the dichotomous dependent variable does not capture the scope or magnitude of innovation
the study does not differentiate between the stages of the innovation process in which obstacles occur

estimator.value: Endogenous switching regression model (Lokshin & Sajaia, 2004) estimated with the two-step consistent estimator: a probit selection equation for facing obstacles (Eq. (3)) and regime-specific innovation equations (Eqs. (1) and (2)) augmented with the inverse Mills ratio

fixed_effects: 22 industry dummies, standard industry grouping by Statistics Denmark (DB07, the Danish version of NACE rev. 2, defined at the six-digit level)
controls: age diversity: standard deviation of age within the firm, 2015
tenure diversity: standard deviation of tenure within the firm, 2015
inverse Mills ratio from the probit selection equation (Eq. (3))
estimation.weights: Unweighted. The firms are selected for the sample by being stratified according to their size, industry, previous R&D expenditure and the variance of previous R&D expenditure; instead of weighting, these variables are included as controls.

ambiguities: The point estimate is positive but not statistically different from zero at the 10 % level; the paper reads this as no effect, so sign is recorded as 'null' rather than 'positive'.

identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables: the treatment is not instrumented and identification of the skill-intensity coefficient rests on the included controls, while the endogenous switching model corrects only for selection into the obstacle regime. A reader could instead class the design as 'other'.

evidence.how: The printed coefficient is the slope on Skill intensity in the linear index of Eq. (2); its units follow from the definition of that regressor and of the dependent variable. No unit conversion was applied.

Table A4, panel 'All innovation', reports the share of firms innovating by obstacle regime and skill-intensity quartile. The value taken here is the cell for firms not facing obstacles in the lowest skill-intensity group (->0.12), i.e. the mean of this outcome at the bottom of the treatment distribution; the paper prints no pooled control-group mean for either regime.

timing.value: Measured in 2015, the year preceding the 2016-2018 window over which the innovation outcome and obstacles are reported, written skill_{it-3} in Eqs. (1)-(3).

definition.value: Takes the value 1 if the firm has introduced service innovations and 0 if the firm has not undertaken any innovation activities; constructed in the same way as product innovation. Survey item Inpdsv: 'Introduced a new or significantly improved service into the market'.

timing.value: Reported in the 2018 wave of the Community Innovation Survey for the period 2016-2018.

units.value: change in the probability of innovation per one-unit increase in the share of workers with a tertiary degree in other fields

estimand.time_horizon: Innovation outcomes over 2016-2018, with skill intensity and the other firm characteristics measured in 2015 (one to three years earlier).

population.description: Danish manufacturing and service firms in the 2018 wave of the Community Innovation Survey merged with Statistics Denmark register data, excluding firms with no declared intention to innovate and firms lacking educational or other information used in the analysis; here firms that face at least one obstacle to innovation (the obstacles = 1 regime, Eq. (1)), on firms that either introduced a service innovation or undertook no innovation activities.
population.period: Innovation outcomes and obstacles 2016-2018; firm and worker characteristics 2015; earlier CIS waves 2006-2015 used for the willingness-to-innovate screen.
subgroups_defined: firms facing obstacles vs firms not facing obstacles
technical vs social sciences/business vs other educational background
all vs product vs service vs process innovation
population.selection: Statistics Denmark draws the CIS sample as a representative, stratified sample of all Danish firms (stratified by firm size, industry and past R&D expenditure, level and variance). Firms with no declared intention to innovate (12 % of the original sample) and firms lacking educational or other information were then dropped, leaving 2223 firms; this column conditions further on firms that face at least one obstacle to innovation (the obstacles = 1 regime, Eq. (1)).

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between firms in the share of their 2015 workforce with tertiary education, within 22 industries and conditional on firm characteristics. There is no reform, lottery or discontinuity; the endogenous switching regression (Lokshin & Sajaia, 2004) corrects only for the non-random selection of firms into the regime of facing obstacles, via a probit selection equation and an inverse Mills ratio.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the included firm characteristics, the 22 industry dummies and (in the innovation equations) the inverse Mills ratio, lagged skill intensity, other educational background is independent of the unobserved determinants of service innovation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No direct test. The paper argues that lagging the explanatory variables to 2015 reduces simultaneity bias and that controlling for industry already accounts for unobserved industry-specific differences related to both skill intensity and innovation.

rhs: unobserved determinants of Service innovation

key_assumptions.assumption: Facing obstacles is endogenous, so each regime's estimation sample is selected; the innovation-equation errors are allowed to covary with the obstacle-equation error and the selection is corrected by the inverse Mills ratio from the probit Eq. (3).

implies_edges.to: estimation sample conditioned on the obstacle regime

formal.as_written: Cov(ε1it, uit) = σ1u ≠ 0 and Cov(ε0it, uit) = σ0u ≠ 0

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction for the selection correction: ln(sales), import share, collaboration with universities and with consultants, and the nine Lerner-index dummies determine the probability of facing obstacles but do not enter the innovation equations directly.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 4 argues that the HHI affects innovation but not whether a firm faces obstacles, while a high Lerner index (low profit margin) affects whether firms face obstacles; no formal test of the exclusion is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The explanatory variables are predetermined: skill intensity and the other firm characteristics are measured in 2015, before the 2016-2018 innovation window, so innovation outcomes do not cause the measured skill intensity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the reason for using lagged explanatory variables; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on firms having a declared intention to innovate; firms with no innovation activities or obstacles in 2016-2018 and no innovation activities in 2006-2018 are dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A7 column 1 re-estimates the model without deleting firms that are not willing to innovate and reports the same findings.

implies_edges.to: estimation sample conditioned on willingness to innovate

key_assumptions.assumption: Distributional and functional assumptions of the endogenous switching model: a linear index in each equation and joint normality of the error terms, as required by the probit selection equation and the inverse-Mills-ratio correction.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the two-step consistent estimator of Heckman (1979) is used and that the findings are the same under full maximum likelihood; the distributional assumption itself is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is a stratified draw: Statistics Denmark selects CIS firms by size, industry and past R&D expenditure, and the regressions are run unweighted with the stratification variables included as controls.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 1 and footnote 7; footnote 7 reports that weighted versions of Tables 6 to 8 give similar results.

population.period: Innovation outcomes and obstacles 2016-2018; firm and worker characteristics 2015; earlier CIS waves 2006-2015 used for the willingness-to-innovate screen.
subgroups_defined: firms facing obstacles vs firms not facing obstacles

all vs product vs service vs process innovation
population.selection: Statistics Denmark draws the CIS sample as a representative, stratified sample of all Danish firms (stratified by firm size, industry and past R&D expenditure, level and variance). Firms with no declared intention to innovate (12 % of the original sample) and firms lacking educational or other information were then dropped, leaving 2223 firms; this column conditions further on firms that do not face obstacles to innovation (the obstacles = 0 regime, Eq. (2)).

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between firms in the share of their 2015 workforce with tertiary education, within 22 industries and conditional on firm characteristics. There is no reform, lottery or discontinuity; the endogenous switching regression (Lokshin & Sajaia, 2004) corrects only for the non-random selection of firms into the regime of facing obstacles, via a probit selection equation and an inverse Mills ratio.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the included firm characteristics, the 22 industry dummies and (in the innovation equations) the inverse Mills ratio, lagged skill intensity, short-cycle tertiary education is independent of the unobserved determinants of process innovation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No direct test. The paper argues that lagging the explanatory variables to 2015 reduces simultaneity bias and that controlling for industry already accounts for unobserved industry-specific differences related to both skill intensity and innovation.

rhs: unobserved determinants of Process innovation

key_assumptions.assumption: Facing obstacles is endogenous, so each regime's estimation sample is selected; the innovation-equation errors are allowed to covary with the obstacle-equation error and the selection is corrected by the inverse Mills ratio from the probit Eq. (3).

key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 4 argues that the HHI affects innovation but not whether a firm faces obstacles, while a high Lerner index (low profit margin) affects whether firms face obstacles; no formal test of the exclusion is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The explanatory variables are predetermined: skill intensity and the other firm characteristics are measured in 2015, before the 2016-2018 innovation window, so innovation outcomes do not cause the measured skill intensity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the reason for using lagged explanatory variables; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A7 column 1 re-estimates the model without deleting firms that are not willing to innovate and reports the same findings.

implies_edges.to: estimation sample conditioned on willingness to innovate

key_assumptions.assumption: Distributional and functional assumptions of the endogenous switching model: a linear index in each equation and joint normality of the error terms, as required by the probit selection equation and the inverse-Mills-ratio correction.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the two-step consistent estimator of Heckman (1979) is used and that the findings are the same under full maximum likelihood; the distributional assumption itself is not tested.

population.description: Danish manufacturing and service firms in the 2018 wave of the Community Innovation Survey merged with Statistics Denmark register data, excluding firms with no declared intention to innovate and firms lacking educational or other information used in the analysis; here firms that do not face obstacles to innovation (the obstacles = 0 regime, Eq. population.period: Innovation outcomes and obstacles 2016-2018; firm and worker characteristics 2015; earlier CIS waves 2006-2015 used for the willingness-to-innovate screen.

money vs knowledge vs market obstacles
short- vs medium- vs long-cycle tertiary education
population.selection: Statistics Denmark draws the CIS sample as a representative, stratified sample of all Danish firms (stratified by firm size, industry and past R&D expenditure, level and variance). Firms with no declared intention to innovate (12 % of the original sample) and firms lacking educational or other information were then dropped, leaving 2223 firms; this column conditions further on firms that do not face obstacles to innovation (the obstacles = 0 regime, Eq. (2)).

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between firms in the share of their 2015 workforce with tertiary education, within 22 industries and conditional on firm characteristics. There is no reform, lottery or discontinuity; the endogenous switching regression (Lokshin & Sajaia, 2004) corrects only for the non-random selection of firms into the regime of facing obstacles, via a probit selection equation and an inverse Mills ratio.

(1)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: No direct test. The paper argues that lagging the explanatory variables to 2015 reduces simultaneity bias and that controlling for industry already accounts for unobserved industry-specific differences related to both skill intensity and innovation.

rhs: unobserved determinants of Innovation (innovation outcome as in Eq. (1))

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction for the selection correction: ln(sales), import share, collaboration with universities and with consultants, and the nine Lerner-index dummies determine the probability of facing obstacles but do not enter the innovation equations directly.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 4 argues that the HHI affects innovation but not whether a firm faces obstacles, while a high Lerner index (low profit margin) affects whether firms face obstacles; no formal test of the exclusion is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The explanatory variables are predetermined: skill intensity and the other firm characteristics are measured in 2015, before the 2016-2018 innovation window, so innovation outcomes do not cause the measured skill intensity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the reason for using lagged explanatory variables; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the two-step consistent estimator of Heckman (1979) is used and that the findings are the same under full maximum likelihood; the distributional assumption itself is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is a stratified draw: Statistics Denmark selects CIS firms by size, industry and past R&D expenditure, and the regressions are run unweighted with the stratification variables included as controls.
